messages.author: 46c154617e9fd110
messages.subject: Standard errors for defined parameters
parts:
Hi everyone,

I was hoping someone could shed some light on estimating standard errors for user-defined parameters in lavaan.

I'm trying to estimate a direct and an indirect effect in a simple path model of the form

A -> B -> C
A -> C

There is also an additional set of covariates that affect both B and C (but not A).


I am using the following syntax:

SEM.model <- 'C ~ beta31*A + beta32*B + [covariates...]
B ~ beta21*A + [the same covariates...]
direct := beta31
indirect := beta21*beta32'

SEM.fit <- sem(SEM.model,
               data=dataset,
               estimator="WLSMV")

summary(SEM.fit, nd=5)


My question is:
Is this syntax correct for obtaining standard errors on the parameters 'direct' and 'indirect'? The standard errors I obtain are much smaller for the indirect effect than for the direct effect (factor of ~5). It's possible there is an empirical reason for this, but prima facie it seems odd.

I'd be very grateful for any help you have to offer.

Best wishes,
Jono

messages.author: 99a06696c483481a
messages.subject: Re: Standard errors for defined parameters
parts:
Jono--
     You can calculate this for yourself. Way back when, Kenny & Judd (1984), developing a method for estimating interaction models, shared a formula for the variance of the product of two normal variables A and B:

variance (A*B) = variance(A) * variance(B) + covariance(A,B)^2 [squared]

Your parameter estimates are (asymptotically) normally distributed under ML estimation, so you just need the covariance matrix of the parameter estimates, which you can obtain from lavaan--see this very helpful page

http://www.quantpsy.org/interact/acov.htm  

--using the vcov() function. If your results are in an object called "fit," then

vcov(fit)

will get you that covariance matrix. Then you could calculate the variance of the product itself. To turn that into a standard error, take the square root and divide by a modifier based on n. You can see from the variances of the original parameters and the reported standard errors how lavaan generates standard errors foe the other parameters. Apply the same modifier to the square root of the variance for the product of parameter estimates, and you should get the standard error that lavaan reports, assuming that you have asked for regular asymptotic standard errors and not bootstrap standard errors.

messages.author: 46c154617e9fd110
messages.subject: Re: Standard errors for defined parameters
parts:
Dear Edward,

Many thanks for your very helpful reply, which seems to provide the means both to check lavaan's output and to analyse why the standard errors for the direct and indirect effects differ so much.

I had a bit of trouble comparing your suggestion to lavaan's output (I hope I'm not being too dense). Repeating the main code for readability:

SEM.model <- 'C ~ beta31*A + beta32*B + [covariates...]
B ~ beta21*A + [the same covariates...]
direct := beta31
indirect := beta21*beta32'

SEM.fit <- sem(SEM.model,
               data=dataset,
               estimator="WLSMV")

summary(SEM.fit, nd=5)

For convenience, let us now set:

V <- vcov(SEM.fit)

For the direct effects, lavaan's standard errors are identical to the the square roots of the diagonal elements of V (so far, so good I think?) These are given by:

sqrt(V[1,1])    # for beta31
sqrt(V[2,2])    # for beta32
sqrt(V[7,7])    # for beta21

Implementing the formula from Kenny & Judd (1984), the standard error for beta21*beta32 should be:

sqrt(V[2,2]*V[7,7]+V[2,7]^2)

I didn't apply a modifier because lavaan's standard errors exactly matched the square root of the diagonal elements for the direct effect, is that correct? The result is much smaller than lavaan's estimated standard error (factor of ~10, so about 50 times smaller than the SE for the direct effect).

Any idea what might be going on here?

Thanks again for your help!

Jono

messages.author: 99a06696c483481a
messages.subject: Re: Standard errors for defined parameters
parts:
Jono--
     I'm not sure, but I wanted to make this more concrete and reproducible. Here is some syntax. I hope this example looks something like what you are seeing:

library("MASS", lib.loc="C:/Program Files/R/R-3.6.1/library")
popcov<-matrix(c(1,.3, .5,.3, 1, .3, .5, .3, 1), nrow=3,byrow=T,dimnames=list(c("x","w","y"),c("x","w","y")))
popcov
popmean<-matrix(c(0,0,0),nrow=3)
data<-mvrnorm(n=500,mu=popmean,Sigma=popcov) # I should have used a seed here for max reproducibility
# and maybe smaller n would produce a greater disparity in results
library("lavaan", lib.loc="~/R/win-library/3.6")
mediat.mod<-'y ~ a*w+c*x
              w ~ b*x
              indirect := a*b'
mediat.out<-sem(mediat.mod,data)
summary(mediat.out)
print(inspect(mediat.out,"vcov"),nd=7)
sqrt(.0014310*.0017164)

In this example, the coefficients a and b have covariance 0 to 7 decimal places, so the calculated variance of the product does not include the covariance squared term. I get a calculated standard error for the defined parameter which is a bit larger than the lavaan-reported value (about 0.15 vs 0.13).
     Still, I am also wondering myself whether lavaan's reported standard errors for defined parameter estimates are correct, and how to check that.

parts:
Hi, 

Standard errors in this case are calculated by the first-order delta method http://lavaan.ugent.be/tutorial/mediation.html.

For example, the gradient for the indirect effect is (b,a,0). Thus, the corresponding standard error is sqrt(t(c(b,a,0))*vcov*c(b,a,0)).

I have calculated the standard error for the indirect effect using data generated by Edward (but with popmean <- matrix(c(3,-1,0),nrow=3) and n=5000, set.seed=1234). 
My standard error =0.01864181, and the standard error returned by lavvan is 0.019 (see code below)


library("MASS")

popcov<-matrix(c(1,.3, .5,.3, 1, .3, .5, .3, 1), nrow=3,byrow=T,dimnames=list(c("x","w","y"),c("x","w","y")))
popcov

popmean <- matrix(c(3,-1,0),nrow=3)
 
library("lavaan")


# Simulation: sample size = 5000

set.seed(1234)

data<-mvrnorm(n=500,mu=popmean,Sigma=popcov)

mediat.mod<-'y ~ a*w+c*x
              w ~ b*x
              indirect := a*b'

mediat.out<-sem(mediat.mod,data)
summary(mediat.out)
print(inspect(mediat.out,"vcov"),nd=7)

grad = c( 0.416,0.205,0) 
vcov = diag(c(0.0015161,0.0020261,0.0017979)); vcov[1,3]=-0.0006302; vcov[3,1]=vcov[1,3]

(my.se.IE = sqrt(t(grad)%*%vcov%*%grad))


Best regards,
Mariia

Op di 12 mei 2020 om 15:12 schreef Edward Rigdon <edward...@gmail.com>:

Jono--
     You can calculate this for yourself. Way back when, Kenny & Judd (1984), developing a method for estimating interaction models, shared a formula for the variance of the product of two normal variables A and B:

variance (A*B) = variance(A) * variance(B) + covariance(A,B)^2 [squared]

http://www.quantpsy.org/interact/acov.htm

vcov(fit)

will get you that covariance matrix. Then you could calculate the variance of the product itself. To turn that into a standard error, take the square root and divide by a modifier based on n. You can see from the variances of the original parameters and the reported standard errors how lavaan generates standard errors foe the other parameters. Op di 12 mei 2020 om 15:12 schreef Edward Rigdon <edward...@gmail.com>:
Jono--
     You can calculate this for yourself. Way back when, Kenny & Judd (1984), developing a method for estimating interaction models, shared a formula for the variance of the product of two normal variables A and B:

variance (A*B) = variance(A) * variance(B) + covariance(A,B)^2 [squared]

Your parameter estimates are (asymptotically) normally distributed under ML estimation, so you just need the covariance matrix of the parameter estimates, which you can obtain from lavaan--see this very helpful page

http://www.quantpsy.org/interact/acov.htm  

--using the vcov() function. If your results are in an object called "fit," then

vcov(fit)

will get you that covariance matrix. Then you could calculate the variance of the product itself. To turn that into a standard error, take the square root and divide by a modifier based on n. You can see from the variances of the original parameters and the reported standard errors how lavaan generates standard errors foe the other parameters. Apply the same modifier to the square root of the variance for the product of parameter estimates, and you should get the standard error that lavaan reports, assuming that you have asked for regular asymptotic standard errors and not bootstrap standard errors.

variance/covariance matrix of the 'defined' variables.

An alternative is to use the bootstrap.
